MonitoringProgramDescription:
Large trees, more than 36 inches in diameter at breast height, are the backbone of an old forest. They store the most carbon, survive low-intensity fire behind thick bark, and give nesting and denning sites to wildlife such as the California spotted owl, northern goshawk, and Pacific marten.

Comstock-era logging cut most of the Basin's large trees in the late 1800s. The trees that escaped it, and the forest that has grown since, set how much old forest structure the Basin has today. Counting large trees over time shows whether that structure is recovering or being lost to drought, insects, and severe fire.
MonitoringApproach:
Individual trees were mapped across the Basin from airborne LiDAR flown in 2010, with each tree's diameter estimated from its LiDAR measurements. The layer holds the 84,373 trees estimated at more than 36 inches.

The map counts the trees in hexagons of 100 acres each. The count will be repeated with the next Basin-wide LiDAR flight, so the change in large trees can be measured.
